newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian PM vows cabinet reshuffle, more reforms.
newsitem.headline: Russian PM vows cabinet reshuffle, more reforms.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, smarting from charges his government cannot tackle Russia's deep economic and social problems, said on Tuesday he would reshape his team and vowed to step up reforms.

His decision followed stern words from President Boris Yeltsin that the government was losing the support of ordinary Russians but the communist opposition warned that a mere cabinet reshuffle would not be enough to win back the nation's trust.
"We are preparing (cabinet changes), they will not only be cosmetic. We are talking of...a deepening of economic reforms," Chernomyrdin said.
"There has been no let-up in the course of reforms, there can be no question of that," he added.

Last weekend Chernomyrdin's liberal predecessor, Yegor Gaidar, who launched market reforms in 1992 by freeing prices, said the prime minister was pushing the country into crisis with inconsistent policies and called for a new government.
On Monday Yeltsin told Chernomyrdin in remarks broadcast on television that some ministers may have to go to help quell rising social strife and to make the government more efficient.
"Maybe we need some people to be changed in the government," said Yeltsin, back in the Kremlin after convalescing from pneumonia and heart surgery.
Non-payment of wages and pensions is one major reason for the government's unpopularity.
Locked in a web of debt, many firms say they cannot pay their workers because their suppliers do not pay them on time. The government blames tax dodgers for its cash shortages.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is bankrolling reforms with a $10 billion three-year loan but on Tuesday said it was not yet ready to hand over more cash.
The IMF is worried about low tax revenues and delays in restructuring Soviet-era industrial plants.
Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, who lost to Yeltsin in last summer's presidential election, said on Tuesday that reshuffling ministers would not address Russia's real problems.

"We insist on a government of popular trust," he told reporters, suggesting that opposition politicians should be brought into the cabinet. He added March would be a month of "big changes" in Russian politics.
Zyuganov warned Yeltsin against trying to bring his chief-of-staff, liberal Anatoly Chubais, back into the government. "This would be the most vile development," he said.
Chubais, who spearheaded Russia's huge privatisation campaign, is a hate figure for the communist and nationalist opposition who dominate the Duma.
They say he amassed huge personal power during Yeltsin's long sickness and absence from the Kremlin and also accuse him of financial irregularities. Chubais denies the charges.
Cabinet spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov said the first government changes could be announced on March 6, the day that Yeltsin makes his annual address to parliament.
Despite the spate of criticisms, Chernomyrdin's own position does not seem to be in serious doubt at present.
"There has been no word about sacking the prime minister," Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Interfax news agency on Monday.
The liberal daily Izvestiya noted that Chernomyrdin was a political survivor whose imminent demise had often been wrongly forecast since he took office more than four years ago.

"We cannot rule out the possibility that the present wave of rumours about his dismissal may be intended to put the premier in his place after he acquired too much independence during the president's illness," Izvestiya added.

Chernomyrdin, 59, took on many of Yeltsin's duties during the president's long absence from the Kremlin before and after last November's heart surgery and January's bout of pneumonia. He is seen as a possible contender for the presidency after Yeltsin retires.
